problem: Session 114 got a single container running in isolation. Real tooling is rarely one container — the ethics- triage script needs to reach a database, an internal API needs to be reachable from the CEx dashboard, and a monitoring agent needs to reach both without being reachable from the open internet. The moment you have more than one container, you have a networking problem: who can talk to whom, on what port, and how does traffic from outside actually find its way in?

Get this wrong and you get one of two failure modes: containers that can't reach each other at all (a service is 'up' but nothing can use it), or containers that are far more exposed than intended (an internal-only database container reachable from the public internet because a port was published carelessly). Container networking is where a lot of accidental security incidents in cloud-native environments actually originate.
concept: Container networking is how Docker gives each container its own isolated network stack (via the NET namespace from Session 114) and then selectively connects those stacks — to each other, to the host, and to the outside world.
Docker ships with several network drivers, each solving a different connectivity problem:

Driver What it connects bridge (default) Containers on the same host, via a private virtual switch host Container shares the host's network stack directly — no isolation none No networking at all — fully isolated overlay Containers across multiple hosts (used by Docker Swarm / multi-node setups) macvlan Container gets its own MAC address, appears as a physical device on the LAN For a single-host setup — which is where most internal CEx tooling would start — the two you'll actually use day to day are the default bridge network and custom user-defined bridge networks.
deep: The default bridge When Docker installs, it creates a virtual switch called docker0 on the host. Every container attached to the default bridge gets a private IP (typically in the 172.17.0.0/16 range), and Docker sets up iptables NAT rules so those containers can reach the outside world, and so specific ports can be published to the host.

The default bridge has a real limitation: containers on it can only reach each other by IP address, not by name, and by default every container on it can reach every other one — there's no segmentation.

User-defined bridge networks — the practical default Creating a custom bridge network gives you two things the default bridge doesn't: automatic DNS resolution by container name, and the ability to isolate groups of containers from each other by simply not attaching them to the same network.

docker network create cex-internal docker run -d --name ethics-db --network cex-internal postgres:16 docker run -d --name ethics-api --network cex-internal my-api:1.0 # Inside ethics-api's container, this now just works:

# psql -h ethics-db -U app -d ethics Publishing ports — controlling inbound access A container's ports are closed to the host and the outside world by default. -p (publish) explicitly maps a host port to a container port; without it, only other containers on the same Docker network can reach that service.
docker run -d --name ethics-api -p 8080:80 --network cex-internal my-api:1.0 # host:container # Now reachable at http://<host-ip>:8080 from outside Docker entirely.
# ethics-db above was NOT published — it's reachable only from # other containers on cex-internal, never from the host or internet.

The rule that prevents most incidents Only publish (-p) the containers that genuinely need to be reached from outside Docker. A database container should almost never have a published port — it should only be reachable from the application containers on its private network.
workflow: Applied to a realistic multi-container CEx tool — say, the ethics-triage container from Session 114, now paired with a small Postgres database to store historical results instead of writing everything back to a Sheet on every run:
1. Create a dedicated network so this tool's containers are isolated from anything else running on the same host: docker network create ethics-net.
2. Start the database container on that network, with no published port — it should never be reachable except from the triage container.
3. Start the triage container on the same network, referencing the database by its container name (ethics-db) rather than an IP — Docker's embedded DNS resolves that automatically.
4. If a small dashboard needs to show results, run it as a third container on the same network, and publish only its port to the host.
5. Verify isolation: from the host, confirm you cannot connect to the database port directly, only to the dashboard's published port.

This mirrors, at a much smaller scale, the same principle behind not exposing your KYC and refund- processing logic directly to the internet — only the front door (the dashboard) is reachable; everything behind it talks over a private network.
enterprise: At enterprise scale, container networking is layered and far more elaborate than a single host's bridge networks, but the same principle — segment by trust boundary, only publish what must be reached — scales up directly.

Scale Networking mechanism Same principle as single-host Docker Single host Docker bridge networks Isolate by network membership Multi-host cluster Overlay networks (Swarm) or CNI plugins (Kubernetes) Isolate by namespace / network policy Kubernetes Services + NetworkPolicies Only expose Services intentionally;

deny-by-default policies Cloud VPCs, subnets, security groups Same segmentation logic, one layer up the stack This is why Layer 3 (Networking) and Layer 4 (Identity) content from earlier in this Knowledge Map keeps resurfacing: container networking, Kubernetes networking, and cloud VPC networking are all the same underlying idea — segmentation and controlled exposure — implemented at different layers.
dependencies: Docker Engine's networking subsystem, which itself depends on the Linux kernel's NET namespaces (Session 114) and iptables/netfilter for NAT and port publishing.
Docker's embedded DNS server (127.0.0.11 inside each container) for name-based resolution on user-defined networks.
The host's own network stack and firewall rules — Docker inserts iptables rules automatically, which can interact unexpectedly with a host firewall (ufw, firewalld) configured separately.
For anything beyond a single host: an overlay network technology (VXLAN, typically) to carry container traffic across hosts.
dependents: docker-compose, which creates a dedicated network for every project automatically, giving each service in a compose file name-based DNS resolution to every other service.
Kubernetes networking (Session covered in Layer 8 later, and Service Mesh at Session 121) — conceptually an evolution of the same bridge-and-DNS pattern, at cluster scale.
Reverse proxies and load balancers placed in front of containers (tying back to Layer 5, Sessions 74–75) — they depend on knowing exactly which container ports are safely publishable.
Multi-container application architectures generally — nothing in a microservices design works without reliable container-to-container networking.
security: Risk Mitigation Publishing a port that should stay internal Default to no -p; add it only when a container must be reached from outside Docker All containers on one flat default bridge Use custom networks to segment by trust boundary (e.g. db-tier vs. app-tier) Binding a published port to 0.0.0.0 unintentionally Bind to 127.0.0.1:8080:80 when the service should only be reachable locally Relying on container IPs, which change on restart Use container names for DNS resolution instead of hardcoded IPs Host firewall not accounting for Docker's iptables rules Understand that Docker can bypass ufw/firewalld rules by inserting its own iptables chains — verify actual exposure with a port scan, not just firewall config For anything in the CEx tooling chain that touches KYC or refund data, the database container should be a textbook case of 'never published, only reachable from the one application container that needs it' — exactly the network-segmentation instinct from Layer 6 (Zero Trust, Least Privilege) applied at container scale.
troubleshooting: Symptom Likely Cause First Command Container A can't reach container B by name Not on the same user-defined network docker network inspect <network> "port is already allocated" Host port already bound by another process/container docker ps --filter publish=<port> Service unreachable from outside Docker Port never published, or bound to wrong interface docker port <container> Container has no internet access DNS misconfiguration or network driver set to none docker exec <container> cat /etc/resolv.conf Symptom Likely Cause First Command Two containers on default bridge can't resolve each other by name Default bridge has no embedded DNS — expected behavior Move both to a user-defined network Unexpected external access to an internal service Port published when it shouldn't have been docker inspect <container> | grep -A5 PortBindings docker network inspect <network> is the single most useful command here — it lists every container attached, their IPs, and confirms whether the segmentation you intended is actually in place.
example: A realistic pattern for a CEx-scale internal tool: an API container that agents' browsers talk to, a worker container that does the heavier processing (NLP on ethics emails, refund calculations), and a database container storing results — three containers, three trust levels.

The API container is the only one with a published port, and even that is typically placed behind a reverse proxy handling TLS termination rather than exposed directly. The worker and database containers sit on an internal-only network, reachable exclusively from the API container, mirroring exactly the segmentation pattern you'd expect from any production system handling financial and identity data.

Pattern to notice The number of published ports in a well-designed multi-container system is almost always small — often just one, at the reverse proxy. Everything else communicates over private, unpublished container networks.
cloud: Cloud container platforms replace Docker's bridge networks with their own managed networking layer, but the segmentation principle is identical:

Platform Networking equivalent Google Cloud Run Ingress settings (internal-only, internal+load-balancer, or all) replace port publishing Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) Services and Ingress objects, backed by VPC-native networking AWS ECS/Fargate Security groups per task, attached to a VPC subnet Azure Container Apps Ingress rules scoped to VNet or external On Cloud Run specifically — the most likely landing spot for CEx tooling given the existing Google stack — a service can be set to 'internal only,' reachable exclusively from within the same Google Cloud VPC or from other Google services, which is the cloud-native equivalent of never publishing a container's port to the host.
automation: docker-compose is where container networking becomes something you declare once rather than wire up manually with docker network create and docker run flags every time:
- "8080:80" # only this service is published networks: [cex-net] db:
image: postgres:16 networks: [cex-net] # no ports: section -> never published networks:

Compose automatically creates cex-net, attaches both services, and gives api name-based resolution to db — the exact multi-step manual workflow from earlier in this session, collapsed into one file that's version-controlled and reproducible.
career: Container networking is where a lot of candidates who know 'Docker basics' actually fall short in interviews — being able to explain why a database shouldn't have a published port, or how DNS resolution works on a user-defined bridge, signals real hands-on experience rather than tutorial-level familiarity.

It's also directly transferable: the segmentation logic here (private network for backend services, one public-facing entry point) is the same logic tested in networking and security interviews generally, just expressed through Docker's vocabulary instead of VLANs or subnets.

misconceptions: Misconception Reality Containers on the same host can always reach each other Only if they share a Docker network — isolation is the default Not publishing a port makes a container fully secure It's unreachable from outside Docker, but still reachable from anything else on its network — network segmentation still matters Container IPs are stable and safe to hardcode They can change on restart; use container names via DNS instead The default bridge network is fine for production It lacks DNS resolution and segmentation; use user- defined networks A host firewall (ufw) fully controls what's exposed Docker inserts its own iptables rules that can bypass ufw's expectations
anchors: Default bridge = no names, no segmentation, everyone can reach everyone. User-defined bridge = names work, and you choose who's on it.
-p (publish) is a door to the outside world — only add it to the container that genuinely needs one.
Container name = the modern way to reach another container. IP address = the way that breaks on restart.
One published port at the front door, private networks for everything behind it — the shape of almost every well-designed multi-container app.

lab: Hands-on: build the 3-container segmented topology described above, using the ethics-triage container from Session 114's lab as the 'worker.'
13. Create a dedicated network: docker network create ethics-net.
14. Start a Postgres container on it with no published port: docker run -d --name ethics-db -- network ethics-net -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=devpass postgres:16.
15. Modify (or stub) the ethics-triage script to connect to host ethics-db instead of writing to a CSV, and rebuild the image from Session 114.
16. Run the triage container on the same network, with no published port either.
17. Build a tiny one-endpoint API (Python/Flask is fine) that queries ethics-db and returns a JSON summary; containerize it and run it on ethics-net WITH a published port: -p 8080:80.
18. Verify from the host: curl localhost:8080 succeeds, but a direct attempt to reach the database port from the host fails.
19. Run docker network inspect ethics-net and confirm all three containers are listed with their internal IPs and that name resolution works: docker exec <api-container> ping ethics-db.

Production tie-in This exact topology — one published entry point, private network for the rest — is the shape you'd deploy if the ethics-triage tooling ever needed a persistent database instead of writing back to a Sheet.
